The most frequent character in the dataset

questions.explanation: The root node corresponds to the empty prefix (""); child links descending from the root represent the first characters of words.

questions.title: Word termination indicator

questions.title: Sparse alphabet representation

examples.output: HashMap avoids massive null pointer arrays

constraints: Select the single correct option ID.

Hash maps automatically keep the child keys in sorted alphabetical order
A fixed array of 65,536+ pointers per node would consume immense memory for sparse branching
Fixed-size arrays in Java cannot hold references to custom objects

questions.explanation: Unicode has over 65,536 Basic Multilingual Plane characters (and 1,114,112 total codepoints). Allocating arrays of that size per node causes unacceptable memory bloat, whereas a map only stores active transitions.

questions.title: Node count for a single word

O(N * L)

questions.explanation: If no two words share any common prefix, every character of every word creates a distinct node, giving at most N * L + 1 nodes, which is O(N * L).

questions.title: Complete binary trie node count

questions.title: Compressed trie internal nodes
questions.description: In a Compressed Trie (Radix Tree / Patricia Trie), non-branching single-child paths are compressed into single edges labeled by substrings. What structural invariant holds for every internal (non-leaf, non-root) node in a Compressed Trie?

options.text: The depth of every leaf is identical
Every internal node has at least two children
Every internal node stores a complete dictionary word
Every internal node has exactly 26 children

hints: If an internal node had only one child, it would have been compressed into the edge.
questions.explanation: By definition of path compression, any node with degree 1 is merged with its child. Hence every internal node must have a branching factor of at least 2.

questions.title: Search time complexity

O(L)
O(N)

questions.explanation: Finding or rejecting a word of length L takes at most L step-downs from root to leaf, each taking O(1) time with array indexing, so total time is O(L), independent of N.

null

constraints: Count only allocations made in the second call.

questions.title: Preserving prefixes on deletion

Set isEndOfWord = false on the 'e' node

questions.title: Pruning threshold during deletion
questions.description: A Trie contains the words 'dog' and 'door'. You delete 'door'. Bottom-up pruning deletes childless non-terminal nodes. Which node is the highest (closest to the root) that gets pruned (set to null)?

The first 'o' node
The 'r' node only
The second 'o' node

questions.explanation: The first 'o' has child 'g' (from 'dog') and child 'o' (from 'door'). When 'door' is deleted, 'r' is deleted, and the second 'o' becomes childless with no word end, so it is pruned. The first 'o' cannot be pruned because it has child 'g'.

questions.title: Pruned node count on deletion
questions.description: Words ['car', 'care', 'careful', 'card'] are inserted into an empty Trie. We then delete 'careful' with bottom-up cleanup of childless non-word nodes. How many nodes are physically removed from the Trie?

questions.title: Trie vs hash set performance trade-off

Strictly lower memory per character than any hash table
Better CPU cache locality on deep pointer dereferencing
Supporting O(1) worst-case time independent of string length L

hints: Hash sets scatter keys across buckets; tries structure keys by prefixes.
questions.explanation: A Trie naturally organizes keys by common prefixes, making prefix searches, autocomplete, longest common prefixes, and lexicographical iteration trivial in O(L) time, whereas a hash set requires scanning all keys.

questions.title: startsWith vs search condition

startsWith requires the final node to have at least one child
startsWith traverses backwards from the leaf to the root

A Trie guarantees O(1) space complexity on the grid

questions.explanation: A Trie validates prefixes on the fly. As soon as the grid path forms a prefix not present in the Trie, DFS backtracks immediately, pruning thousands of redundant paths.

questions.title: In-place grid cell marking

questions.title: Dynamic leaf pruning in grid search
questions.description: In Word Search II, after a leaf word in the Trie is found, what pruning technique provides the greatest speedup for the remaining grid searches?

questions.title: Trie-accelerated word break
questions.description: In Word Break (determining if string s can be segmented into dictionary words), how does storing the dictionary in a Trie accelerate the DP transition dp[i]?

options.text: By matching characters against the Trie from index j forward, we can break early as soon as a prefix is invalid

questions.title: Double-array trie primary arrays
questions.description: A Double-Array Trie (DAT) compresses trie transitions into two parallel 1D integer arrays, enabling O(1) state transitions with minimal memory overhead. What are the standard names of these two arrays?
constraints: Select the single correct option ID.

options.text: LEFT and RIGHT
BASE and CHECK
PREFIX and SUFFIX
HEAD and TAIL

hints: BASE holds offset values; CHECK validates the origin state.
questions.explanation: In Aoe's Double-Array Trie, BASE[s] provides the base offset for state s, and CHECK[t] verifies that t was reached from s (i.e. CHECK[BASE[s] + c] == s).
